title: Reinforcement Learning: Q-Learning, Deep Q-Learning and SARSA
description: How an agent learns by trial and error through rewards and penalties - and how Q-Learning, Deep Q-Learning and SARSA turn that interaction into optimal policies.
content:
**Reinforcement learning (RL)** is a paradigm in machine learning where an agent learns to make decisions by interacting with an environment. Unlike supervised learning, which relies on labeled datasets, RL centers on the idea of trial-and-error guided by rewards and penalties.

Key components:
• Agent - an autonomous entity that selects actions based on its current state.
• Environment - the world with which the agent interacts.
• State (S) - a representation of the current situation of the environment.
• Action (A) - a decision or move that the agent can make.
• Reward (R) - a numerical signal that indicates the immediate benefit (or cost) of an action.
• Policy - a strategy mapping states to actions with the goal of maximizing the cumulative reward, often discounted over time.

The RL process is an iterative cycle:
• Initialization - the agent and environment are set up.
• Interaction - the agent selects actions based on its current state.
• Feedback - the environment responds with rewards.
• Learning - the agent updates its knowledge (e.g., Q-coefficients) and improves its policy.

**Q-Learning (QL)** is a model-free reinforcement strategy used to find the optimal policy for a finite Markov decision process.

How it works:
• The agent explores the environment by selecting actions based on an exploration–exploitation strategy.
• After each action, the agent updates the Q-coefficients of the current state-action pair using the Bellman equation.
• As the session continues, the Q-coefficients converge to the optimal values, allowing the agent to implement optimal strategies.

**Deep Q-Learning (DQL)** applies Q-Learning ideas to environments with high-dimensional or continuous state spaces, where maintaining an explicit Q-table is impossible.

How it works:
• Instead of a table of Q-coefficients, a deep neural network approximates the Q-function.
• The agent stores its experiences in a replay buffer and trains on random mini-batches.
• This breaks correlations between consecutive experiences and improves convergence.

**SARSA (State-Action-Reward-State-Action)**, unlike Q-Learning (which is off-policy), is on-policy and learns the value of taking actions according to the current policy.

How it works:
• The update is based on the actual action chosen from the next state, instead of the maximum over all possible actions.
• Because SARSA updates its Q-values with the actions actually taken, it often results in a more conservative policy - one that takes into account the cost of exploring when there might be risks in the environment.

**Quick comparison:**
• QL - model-free and off-policy; a Q-table of coefficients updated via the Bellman equation; actions chosen with an exploration–exploitation strategy.
• DQL - a neural network approximates the Q-function for high-dimensional or continuous state spaces; a replay buffer with random mini-batches improves convergence.
• SARSA - on-policy; updates with the action actually taken from the next state; tends to yield a more conservative policy.
